changed_views: Agent adoption can be financed by an established software business before the pricing model is settled. Vanta's reported 25% adoption makes that strategy concrete, while the proposed 75% adoption and retention improvements remain targets.
Domain experts and code structure remain useful assets as models improve: Vanta invests both in expert-authored evaluations and in making legacy components comprehensible to coding agents.

Internal and buyer incentives can delay capable products. At 21:13–22:39, Cacioppo says a motivated team initially chose a familiar onboarding wizard because it feared failure; she reports shipping a file-driven conversational flow after that concern was addressed. At 49:15–49:51, she recounts an enterprise asking to disable AI to simplify procurement and says Vanta declined to build that switch.

Tenex's services opportunity and Cacioppo's skepticism about forward-deployed economics can both be true. Demand for implementation does not establish healthy margins without evidence about delivery cost, reusable work and contract size.
follow_ups: Track agent adoption using a consistent denominator and activity threshold, then compare retention, customer expansion and support burden with matched customers; separate current 25% adoption from the 75% ambition.
Request the inference-cost and gross-margin bridge behind absorbed token costs, and test whether output pricing improves monetization without discouraging useful work.
Look for evaluation coverage, error severity and supervision costs for Vanta's specialized agents, plus measured engineering outcomes after codebase modularization.
Watch for actual security-product releases, supported actions, permission boundaries and pricing; distinguish the described remediation vision from existing compliance automation.
Compare forward-deployed engineering hours and ongoing support costs with contract value and renewals, and track whether reusable implementations improve economics.
Follow compensation and liquidity disclosures with attention to equity valuation and dilution; do not treat the top-pay comparison as a company-wide wage trend.

signals.claim: Cacioppo says Vanta is absorbing token costs and accepting lower margins while roughly 25% of customers use its agent workflow; reaching 75% is a goal, with pricing to be resolved later.
signals.evidence: She argues that marked-up token pricing invites customers to compare an application directly with its underlying model. Vanta is prioritizing usage and expects better retention as agents do more work, but she supplies no measured retention uplift or margin bridge. At 14:39 she also distinguishes charging for completed outputs from true outcomes and says a menu of many billable tasks creates cognitive overhead. The 25% is her approximate current adoption figure; 75% and the commercial payoff are aspirations. Vanta's [September guide](https://help.vanta.com/en/articles/16397022-create-schedule-and-manage-custom-agents) documents scheduled agents with creator permissions and approval gates, but does not verify adoption or retention figures.

signals.claim: Cacioppo says Vanta's model selection is driven by task-specific evaluations written by security and compliance experts, with quality currently taking priority over token cost.
signals.evidence: She describes one customer-facing agent backed by hundreds of specialized agents and says the team invested at the start of the year in evaluation frameworks written by people who had run security programs. Her rationale for emphasizing quality is that Vanta's decision-and-action workloads consume fewer tokens than coding workloads. This is a description of Vanta's evaluation process and relative usage, not a published reliability benchmark or a quantified cross-industry cost comparison. Its [July engineering account](https://www.vanta.com/resources/giving-the-vanta-agent-a-computer) also documents evaluation datasets curated by GRC experts and checks on quality, latency and authorization.

signals.claim: Cacioppo says Vanta is modularizing its eight-year-old codebase so coding agents can understand smaller components fully, reducing dependence on engineers who must supply missing context.
signals.evidence: She describes agents behaving poorly when presented with the entire legacy codebase and requiring a highly knowledgeable engineer to supervise them. The ongoing response combines people and agents to make the code easier to understand. She likens the problem to onboarding many engineers at once. This gives a concrete investment behind agent adoption, but she provides no measured change in defect rate, supervision time or delivery speed.

signals.claim: Cacioppo estimates that total compensation for Vanta's top-paid person is about ten times the level five years earlier, and says competition for people is changing compensation and liquidity expectations.
signals.evidence: The comparison is her response to a question about the highest-paid person across time, not a tenfold raise for every employee or necessarily the same individual. She values people with company and customer context who can make decisions and act, and would prefer more pay dispersion. She says Vanta historically had not done tenders but employees increasingly expect liquidity. Stock compensation and dilution are an explicit counterweight; no pay amounts, valuation adjustment or tender launch is disclosed.

signals.claim: Cacioppo questions whether expensive forward-deployed engineering can be sustained on five- and six-figure contracts, even if the title helps attract exceptional talent.
signals.evidence: She characterizes much of the work as professional services and contrasts smaller contracts with the eight-figure deals she associates with Palantir. This is her assessment of service-delivery economics, without customer-level costs or margins. It does not establish that all forward-deployed teams lose money: the relevant test is engineering effort and reuse relative to contract value and renewal revenue.

signals.claim: Cacioppo positions Vanta's next expansion around automated security remediation for its existing customer base, particularly companies unlikely to buy large-enterprise security products.
signals.evidence: She points to roughly 16,000 customers and integrations with around 400 tools as a foundation for additional products. Her envisioned loop pairs continuous testing with remediation, including cloud misconfiguration work. The suggested $40,000–$50,000 purchase versus a $150,000 alternative illustrates customer segmentation; it is not announced Vanta pricing or a verified competitor quote. At 01:03:03 she expects humans to design rules while more individual decisions move to machines. These are strategic plans, not evidence that a comprehensive autonomous security product is already deployed. The existing [Wiz integration](https://help.vanta.com/en/articles/11345611-connecting-wiz-with-vanta) imports findings for compliance and explicitly does not support write-back, illustrating the boundary of that integration.

summary: Vanta CEO Christina Cacioppo describes a deliberate trade-off between current margins and agent adoption: the company is absorbing token costs while trying to move more customers into workflows where agents prepare and execute work with permission. She reports roughly 25% adoption of that workflow and identifies domain-specific evaluations, codebase modularization and organizational habits as practical constraints. Her account also connects growing compensation for exceptional employees with competition from AI companies, and outlines expansion from compliance into automated security work for existing customers. The operational figures are management estimates; retention gains and broader security automation remain ambitions. Timestamps refer to the [official video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sQaM5oPlUYs), whose edit differs from the podcast audio.
why_it_matters: Vanta offers a concrete example of an established software company financing an agent transition from its existing business. Adoption, inference cost and pricing must be tested together: a lower current margin can fund a better product, but the interview does not establish the eventual retention or monetization payoff. Its accumulated integrations and customer relationships may help distribute security automation, while domain evaluation, engineering context and buyer approval processes still constrain deployment.
